subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
If any argument was
needed, Mr. Speaker, to show the utter failure to bring about its declared objective, the attitude adopted by protectionist advocates in ithis House, certainly shows the absolute failure of the protectionist system to bring about the benefits which its advocates some fifty years ago said would be brought about. Apparently the great theme of the protectionist advocates in this House is a declaration of Canadian incapacity. "We are not able", they say in one breath, "to compete against the low-paid labour of Europe; we are unable to compete against the depreciated currency of Europe". In the next breath they say, "We are unable to compete against the highly-paid and highly-skilled labour of the United States". I think I am on common ground with all the students of the economic history of the country when I say that when fifty years ago or thereabouts, Sir John A. Macdonald, the Hon. C. C. Colby and other leading Conservative Statesmen of that day asked the Canadian people to adopt the principle of protection as the guiding principle of our fiscal policy, they based their appeal on the infant industry argument. They appealed to the people of Canada, and their appeal, I must say, was a somewhat attractive one. They said, "Give our manufacturers a few years of state-aid by way of a tariff, help them to pass through this crisis, and in a very few years, perhaps a score of years, they will be able to stand on their own feet. We will obtain goods just as cheaply as ever, and we will have in addition manufactures established in our country". That was one argument presented to the people of Canada at that date. Another argument that was presented to those who lived in the Maritime provinces at that time was that the tariff was not going to be raised at all, and that it was merely to be a readjustment of the tariff. I take it that had the protagonists of protection in 1876, 1877 and 1878 told the people of Canada that fifty years later, when on many of the necessaries of life the schedule rates

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
ware just as high as they were when first levied the protected manufacturers of this country would be asking for precisely the same rate of tariff protection, the Canadian people never would have given way to their appeals, never would have adopted the protective principle as the guiding principle of their fiscal policy and would not have rejected Alexander Mackenzie in 1878.
I wish to make a very few general observations on certain protectionist arguments that have been presented. I cannot traverse all these assertions. I said a moment ago " arguments", but I think that is rather too complimentary a term to use. I cannot traverse all the protectionist assertions, for the protectionist speeches as a rule have been extravagant in assertion but parsimonious in argument. Let me deal very briefly with two arguments which were adduced yesterday by the eloquent member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion).
In brief, he had two arguments which a hasty perusal of his speech enables me, I trust, to answer. The first argument he brought forward was this:	Appealing to the
historian Macaulay, he said that very great progress had been made between 1685 or 1688, about the time of the great revolution in England of 1688, and 1845. Without doubt, he was perfectly correct in his historical statement based on the words of that well known historian; but then he went on to say:	That shows that Great Britain had
so far developed under a protectionist policy that it was able to march forward by the impetus given by protection and apparently was able to prosper under free trade by reason of the start that the industries had received under protection. Let me say this. Throughout the Middle Ages and right down to almost the middle of the nineteenth century, Great Britain, as well as all other countries in the civilized world, was protectionist. If anything, the protection in Great Britain was considerably less hampering to trade than the protection on the continent. For instance, before the French revolution and, I think, perhaps even thereafter, they had tariffs between different parts of France, and wheat and other grains could not move freely from one part of the Kingdom of France to another. They had-and they have had it until quite recently-a little protective tariff or rather a little tariff for revenue purposes around every town of any considerable size in France. They had protection on the continent; they had protection in Great Britain; but Great Britain started to get rid of protection, I think, earlier than any other country in Europe.

Walpole started the work, in 1750, or thereabouts, Adam Smith wrote his great work; he converted to his views the great minister, Pitt, who started taking off duties, and who would probably have had the tariff almost on a free trade basis had the revolutionary wars with France not intervened. During the whole of the revolutionary and Napoleonic wars from 1763 to 1815, there was no movement' towards freer trade; but after the revolutionary and Napoleonic wars were over, Huskisson started in 1823 to take off duties. He was followed by Peel, so that in 1842 most of the duties on manufactured goods had been taken off. Then the duties on foodstuffs were removed from 1846 to 1849, and finally the work was completed in 1860 by William Ewart Gladstone. From then until 1903 free trade was accepted without question as the guiding principle of British policy.
What led the British people to get rid of duties on food? During the whole of the eighteenth century Great Britain produced about enough food for itself. As a matter of fact, in years of abundance they were able to ship food from England; but by reason of the invention of the steam engine, an invention for which British ingenuity is largely to be credited, and by the fact that there were in Great Britain coal and iron in close proximity, the industrial revolution, which was really unconnected with tariffs, brought about a development in the industrial life in Great Britain sooner than anywhere else in the world. The centre of population moved from the more southerly and easterly counties of . England over towards the north and towards the west, and Lancashire and Yorkshire began to be hives of industry. That was in process before, during and; immediately after the Napoleonic wars. Prior to the time of the revolutionary wars, Great Britain was about able to feed itself, but the development of manufacturing caused a great increase in population. That great increase in population ate up all the food that Great Britain was able to produce, and during the years from 1793 to 1815, while the war kept food from coming to Britain's shores from the continent of Europe, wheat went up to between two and three dollars a bushel. That had the result of raising the rent of land, and when Waterloo occurred and the Peace of Paris brought an end to almost a generation of warfare, the price of wheat fell from three dollars to two dollars a bushel. The landlords, who at that time controlled both the House of Commons and the House of Lords-the landed interest was the paramount interest in Great Britain at that time-were not pleased that the food

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
of the people was being cheapened, because that meant a reduction of their rents, and they combined with the farmers, who had a considerable amount of political power, to place upon the statute books the Com Laws of 1815, which had the result of imposing starvation by law upon a large proportion of the British people when crops were scarce. The whole generation from 1815 to 1845 of what we call the labouring classes, the plain and common people who worked with their hands, protested against that:
Bread taxed Weaver, canst thou see,
What this tax has done for thee?
See thy children vilely led,
Singing hymns for shameful bread,
While the stones of every street,
Know their naked little feet.
That was the condition of Great Britain under protection. They hold out protection as having made Great Britain strong and powerful! Why, in the hungry forties, people were starving by reason of protection, and 1 have had an old Scotchwoman tell me that herself. Aye, and one man out of ten was in receipt of public relief. The people wen working in the coal mines, young girls, young children, women working like beasts of burden to get the pittance with which they had to buy the high priced food of the time. No, it was not protection that made Great Britain great. What made Great Britain great was following a system of freedom, and that is what will make this country great-following a system of freedom and not a system of restriction.
Mr. Speaker, I do not pretend for an instant that free trade is a panacea for everything; that we would have a second heaven on earth in this country if we had free trade. It is only one of the reforms which we need in Canada. As Great Britain has been an outstanding example of the benefits of freedom of commerce, it is quite in line with the protectionist advocates to endeavour to destroy the value of the evidence of British economists, and the eloquent member for Fort William and Rainy River the other day endeavoured to lead us to believe that Mr. John Stuart Mill, the great economist, believed in the infant industry theory. That is not a new dodge on the part of the Conservative party. In 1876, Sir John A. Macdonald quoted these words from John Stuart Mill's Political Economy, the words which were quoted the other night by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River:
The only case in which on mere principles of political economy protecting duties can be defensible is when they are imposed temporarily (especially in a young and rising nation),-	,
One would suppose, of course, that the imposition of duties for almost fifty years war a fair "temporary" trial.
-in hope of naturalizing a foreign industry in itself perfectly suitable to the circumstances of the country. The superiority of one country over another in a branch of production often arises only from having begun it sooner. There may be no inherent advantage on one part, or disadvantage on the other, but only a present superiority of acquired skill and experience. A country which has this skill and experience yet to acquire may in other respects be better adapted to the production than those which were earlier in the field, and besides it is a just remark of Mr. Rae. that nothing has a greater tendency to promote improvements in any branch of production than its trial under a new set of conditions.
That reminds me of a striking instance of the superiority of Canadian over British production, which was cited to me some time ago by a Conservative member, himself a manufacturer. He said that during the war his factory began making shells. After having received from the government payment for the shells on the basis of what it cost in Great Britain to manufacture shells in the government arsenal, they made so much money that as a patriotic citizen he felt that he should reduce the price. Accordingly he cut the price in half and still they made money, so that he decided to reduce it to 25 per cent of the original price. And notwithstanding that reduction they were able to make a profit. True it is that in a new country it may be wise to try out old methods and improve upon them. This argument in regard to production is a two-edged sword: it is -hardly right for people who have that capacity which I have just illustrated to play the part of those to whom state-aid is imperative. To continue:
But it cannot be expected that individuals should at their own risk, or rather to their certain loss, introduce a new manufacture and bear the burthen of carrying it on until the producers have been educated up to the level of those with whom the processes are traditional. A protecting duty, continued for a reasonable time, wiirsometimes be the least inconvenient mode in which the nation can tax itself for the support of such an experiment. But the protection should be confined to cases in which there is good ground of assurance that the industry which it fosters will after a time be able to dispense with it-
That is a clause which must have escaped the attention of the hon. gentleman who quoted John Stuart Mill to the House.
-nor should the domestic producers ever be allowed to expect that it will be continued to them beyond the time necessary for a fair trial of what they are capable of accomplishing.
If protectionists desire to take comfort from that statement they are of course perfectly at liberty to do so; but in considering it they should admit the fact that John Stuart Mill withdrew the statement. We have excellent evidence to substantiate that assertion.
The Budget-Mr. McMaster

Let me read it to you. I take this from a speech delivered by that great leader of his time, the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, than whom a more faithful public servant and a more honest man never ornamented this House of Commons. He said:
But, sir, before proceeding to discuss some of the matters the right hon. gentleman referred to, let me call the attention of everyone for a moment to his remarks regarding John Stuart Mill. The hon. gentleman may not have made the statement that my hon. friend from Waterloo attributed to him, but he may find, if he recalled a certain circumstance, that he might have done so. He must surely remember that even John Stuart Mill wrote a letter to Mr. Greeley, of New York, withdrawing that passage from his book. He may remember the disappointment felt by the protectionists of the United States with reference to Mr. Mill's passages-how they distorted it, when Mr. Mill really withdrew it and expressed his regret that it had ever been put in. But in order to make doubly sure,
I had the pleasure last summer of meeting with a well known English writer-whom the hon. gentleman no doubt knows-Mr. Newmarsh, an intimate friend of Mr. Mill; and I called his attention to this circumstance, sitting at the dinner table one day in London. He said: "Oh, yes; that is well known. We all expressed our exceeding regret to Mr. Mill that the passage should have been written, as it was liable to be misunderstood. He withdrew it, however, unmistakably and completely".
Now I would pass on to the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I am not at all sure whether the views expressed by him are an accurate reflection of the attitude of the Canadian manufacturers generally. I should regret the fact if they were. But if the attitude displayed by the hon. gentleman to-day be an accurate expression of the general sentiment of our manufacturers, what does it indicate? It simply means that they are not prepared in the public interest to give up one shred or one tittle of the special privileges which they now enjoy. There is not one group in this House, there is not one individual member of this assembly, that does not wish for the growth and prosperity of our Canadian manufacturers. But what we are anxious for is that this growth shall not be at the expense of other interests in the country. It was a French economist who said that there is no use arguing with a protectionist because protection is not a philosophy but an appetite, and it is futile arguing with people about their appetites. Sometimes when I reflect upon the history of those who have enjoyed special privileges of any sort I am inclined to agree with this French economist. But is it wise for the possessors of special privileges to hold on to them with too firm a grasp and to refuse to realize the rights and the desires of other people?

If you will pardon another historical allusion, you will remember that before the French revolution the clergy and the nobility had been able to discharge themselves of all responsibility for public burdens while they enjoyed great public privileges; and they held on to those privileges in spite of the warnings of the physiocrats, in spite of the appeals of the philosophers, and in spite of what their own consciences must have told them was right. They clung to those privileges until finally they saw them wiped out over night. I ask the House to compare with that what happened on the other side of the British channel, where there were also great privileges enjoyed by the few. The *landed interest in Great Britain controlled both Houses; and in 1832 the rotten boroughs, practically pocket boroughs, the private property of the great landlords, were in many cases wiped out. Great Britain came almost to the verge of revolution, but that wholesome respect for and fear of their fellow citizens led the British landlords, the British nobility and the British privileged classes generally to give way. Again in 1868 when there was a great movement for the extension of the franchise there were people in Great Britain who were very much put out by the circumstance and desired to prevent the common man from receiving the right to vote; for at that time only about one *man in six enjoyed the franchise. Again, however, in the face of great public agitation, and public meetings addressed by the leaders of the movement to the people assembled in thousands, the opponents of the popular movement yielded. It is wise sometimes to give way. I would recommend an attitude of conciliation, an attitude of endeavouring to appreciate the other fellow's position to the privileged interests of this country.
And now I think I can perhaps best take up the various matters connected with the tariff by following the very interesting speech delivered this afternoon by the member for St. Lawrence-St. George, because I take it that he is regarded in this country as the accredited representative of the big interests. Last year, almost twelve months ago, the hon. member followed me when I spoke in the budget debate; it is my turn now to follow him. On that occasion he made use of these words:
Let me turn to the hon. member for Brome who made a speech this evening, and stated he was absolutely against the principle and practice of protection. No doubt hon. members opposite agree with all he said. They have heard his remarks with reference to hit defection. I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to say

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
very much about the defection of the hon. member for Brome beyond stating it was very regrettable to me that he should have adopted such an attitude towards the party he has followed for so many years. What did the hon. member say? He said he was a Liberal and he was the only man who understood the Liberal doctrine. Well, why does the hon. member for Brome pose as the arbiter of the Liberal party? Can no other hon. members in this House understand what the Liberal doctrine or the Liberal policy is? Why did he say that he, and he alone, is the only man in the House that understands the Liberal doctrine?
The hon. member for Brome is advancing his own personal ideas and views instead of sinking those personal views as many of us have to do for the general good of the country.
Now, I do not propose to administer to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George any reciprocal lecture. I learned at the feet of Sir Wilfrid Laurier that in politics there is no room for resentment On the contrary, I would congratulate the hon. gentleman on his sincerity and courage. If those are the views which he holds-and I believe them to be his sincere views-it is right that he should express them. In the world at present parliamentary representative institutions are on trial. In Italy we see one dictator holding sway; in Spain we see another; we have had rumours that some people in France think they should have a dictator there; and therefore it is for us, who are the inheritors, along with other British countries, of British parliamentary institutions and traditions, to see that those are kept intact and inviolate. One of the things which has destroyed parliamentary government in some countries, and has depreciated its prestige in others, has been the insincerity of public men. I believe that the people of Canada are sick and tired of men who advocate policies in which they do not believe, who advocate one thing at one time and another at another time. And after all the personality of the member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the personality of the member for Brome are nothing in comparison with the importance of the issues which are before the Canadian people today.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George spoke about agricultural implements. But before I deal with that part of his speech I think I should very briefly refer to something on which he had a good deal to say- the Laurier-Fielding tariff. I have been associated with the Liberal party for a good many years, but I never heard about a tariff called the Laurier-Fielding tariff until quite recently. The tariff which obtained in this country for a great many years was introduced by Mr. Fielding in 1897. It did not go as far in the direction of cutting down duties as I would have liked; but it did cut down some. It did introduce the
British preference, first at 121 per cent, in the following year at 25 per cent, and the year after that at 33j per cent. But I take it that those who presented themselves as Liberal candidates in the election of 1921 were not obliged to go back in the far and distant past to find what the declared policy of the Liberal party was. I think that perhaps if they had looked back for the ten years previous to 1921 they could have obtained a just appreciation of what was expected of those who declared themselves to be Liberal candidates. The member whom I congratulate for the pleasant and courteous way in which 'he spoke this afternoon was insistent upon picking out here and there statements of a more or less protectionist nature from speeches delivered by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and by Mr. Fielding. But, strangely enough, he forgot to mention one of the greatest steps towards freedom of commerce which has ever been taken by a political party in this country; that was the attempt to give the people reciprocity in 1911. That episode was conspicuous by its absence from his speech. I think perhaps that here I should make a few brief references to the views of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the last ten years of his life.
In 1911 the Liberal party went to the country on reciprocity. In 1912 I well remember Sir Wilfrid Laurier addressing a great meeting in Montreal and laying down his principles to the effect that he believed in reciprocity and that some day the Canadian people would regret that they had rejected it. From 1911 right up to 1917 the Liberal party, by resolution after resolution in the House of Commons, pledged itself to a reduction of the tariff. After 1917 I had something to do with the expression of Liberal views in this House, and on several occasions, with not the entire support but almost the entire support of the Liberal party of that day, I placed on Hansard resolutions-always voted down by the government of that day-in favour of lower tariffs. In the last few weeks of his life Sir Wilfrid Laurier made a great speech to the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association. What did he say on that occasion? I have quoted from bis speech before, and I do not propose to repeat those quotations now, but here is something that I do not think I placed before the House when I spoke in the debate on the Address. After speaking of the British preferential policy-which now no longer merits the approval of the member for St. Lawrence-St. George-Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
We said, "No; we are not going to bargain with the Mother Country upon matters of that kind."

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
We do it because we are British subjects, and because we believe in the principles of free trade. We believe also it is for the good of the Canadian people that we should adopt that policy, and by that policy we stand to-day also. In your resolution you affirm that the black eye which was given by the present government three years ago should be removed, and, Sir, if it is in our power to do so we shall do so; at all events we shall take the opportunity to bring the matter before parliament at the next session.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not in his later days a protectionist. He was a man. who believed in reduction of tariffs; he was a real Liberal, and he believed that freedom of exchange was part of the Liberal doctrine, of the Liberal tradition. While we were in opposition, after 1917, we had statements from Mr. Fielding himself that protection was not the principle which should guide the fiscal affairs of this country. It is difficult to imagine how a man could present himself as a supporter of the Liberal party and take the stand that duties were not to come down at all. I realize the difficulty in which many members of this House find themselves in connection with the trade question and I realize that the matter has to be dealt with with prudence and with care. I have every sympathy for the man who has protected industries in his riding which are fearful of what may happen, and I am all for prudence, all for conciliation, all for care, in regard to the trade policy. But the direction must be established, and progress must be made in the right direction visible to the naked eye, as I have said on previous occasions.
The hon. member stated that he had some sort of dispensation from some one or other for an apparent disagreement with the main body of the Liberal party on the trade issue. He did not tell us who granted him that dispensation, and I do not care very much who granted it, because the Liberal party, as I understand * it, is not a hierarchy that grants dispensations: we are supposed to hold true to the tradition of the fathers in its entirety. But the hon. gentleman did refer to a very respectable character in the province of Quebec, Mr. Alexandre Taschereau, as one who had made protectionist speeches. I have an admiration for the Hon. Alexandre Taschereau. I had the pleasure last October of going down into the county of Brome and of speaking to my friends there in support of one who was the candidate of the Liberal party in the Quebec House led by the Hon. Alexandre Taschereau. But so far as trade questions are concerned, as far as the fiscal policy of the country is concerned, I decline to admit for an instant that any provincial premier has the right to speak for the Liberal party or

for any other party in the federal arena. The dispensation, if obtained from the Hon. Alexandre Taschereau, was not worth the paper it was written on.
Let me now take up the question of agricultural implements. The hon. member gave a good deal of time to the consideration of agricultural implements. He said that reductions ranged all the way from 4 to 12J per cent and he gave the House to understand, if he dlid1 not say so in so many words, that it would be impossible to carry on agricultural implement manufacturing in Canada without the help of a protective tariff. That is the statement made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, but unfortunately it does not agree with the evidence given before the Drayton Tariff Commission in 1920. I would like to read to the House some evidence given by the then president of the Massey-Harris Company, Mr. Thomas Findley, who, perhaps, may be taken as a better guide as to the feelings and views of the implement manufacturers than the member for St. Lawrence-St. George. He said:
So far as the Massey-Harris Company is concerned, even to-day, placing no other consideration in the scales but that of money making, we should be quite prepared to have the tariff taken off our implements, if at the same time it were taken off everything that enters into the cost of producing them. In fact, considering how large our foreign trade is, in proportion to the whole, we honestly believe we could make more money under such a free trade condition than we are making at the present time.
And he makes this statement:
On August 14, 1917, following a very full discussion of the whole tariff situation and its effect upon our company the following resolution was unanimously passed by our directors and placed upon the minutes of the board:
" A further discussion on the tariff situation followed, and the president submitted figures illustrating the effect of the tariff on our business; and, while the consensus of opinion was that, given free materials, machinery and all other articles entering into the manufacture of our goods and the operation of our plants, we would be as well off with free agricultural implements, it was not thought desirable to make a statement of any kind at present in regard to the position on account of the unsettled political situation and the feeling that the effect of practically free trade on other Canadian manufacturing industries might be different from its effect on ourselves.
Now, it is true that the Canadian, implement manufacturers have not got all that enters into their cost of production free. They have not got free coal, or free steel for the erection of their factories, or free belting or free machinery. But they have got free raw materials; they have got partly at least the condition under which they said free trade would be a benefit to them, and they have not had all the duty

Now I come to fertilizers. This is one of the items on which the tariff has been substantially reduced-in fact it has disappeared, having been reduced from 10 per cent to nothing at all. Of course that is only what it should be. The idea of taxing that which is to restore and renew the fertility of the soil is certainly taxation run mad. But I do not believe that our Canadian manufacturers need! complain very much. The total production for 1922 amounted to $5,533,136. We imported $1,048,620, and we exported $2,213,351. Therefore in 1922 we exported 40 per cent of our entire production. Of course, when we exported we had to meet the competition of the fertilizer manufacturers in the countries into which we sent our goods. Then we had brought before the special committee examining into agricultural conditions by an unimpeachable authority, by one of the members of the committee himself, the fact that a fertilizer company in New Brunswick was able to charge its New Brunswick customers $9 per ton more than it charged its customers for the selfsame thing across the line in, the state of Maine. This tariff, I trust, will go into effect, and consequently next year the New Brunswick farmers will pay the same price as the Maine farmers.
While I was thinking of fertilizers my subconscious mind reminded me of something I had forgotten in regard to agricultural implements, and I crave your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, while I return to that subject for a moment. It is to answer the argument adduced by the member for St. Lawrence-St, George. He asked: What about our people who supply our Canadian manufacturers of implements with their raw material? Well, how much of the raw material is bought in Canada? Mr. Findley, in his evidence before the special committee to which I have already referred, said that two-thirds of the raw material of his company was purchased in the United States; that they got pig iron from Pittsburgh much of their other material of a mineral nature from Buffalo and Tona-
102i
wanda, and all their wood from the United States also. I think it well that these facts should be known.
Now I pass on to another head of my observations. The government have taken a 6tep, and a decided step in the right direction, and any help that I can give them along those lines ^will most readily afford. But I have the feeling that, having started on the right road, they will not mind if a candid friend points out other steps which should be taken at the earliest possible moment. I want to see a modification, if not an entire elimination, of the dumping clause. I think it is an evil thing, and, like most evil things, it likes to work in the dark. I do not think the government quite realize how much they disappointed their friends, before bringing in this budget that we welcome so warmly, when by regulation they did away with the saving paragraph in the dumping clause which prevented its being applied if the difference between the market price and the purchase price was less than 5 per cent. Now, I do not know just what effect that may have. It may not have as much effect as I dread, but I do not like it, and I want to see it removed at the earliest possible moment.
I do not think the public of Canada quite realize what this dumping clause really does, so I am going to try, in the most untechnical language possible, to explain its operations. If I go into the United States, let us say, and buy $100 worth of goods, and the ordinary market price is $100, I come back to the customs house and pay, let us say, 10 per cent- if that is the rate of duty-on that $100 worth of goods, or $10. Suppose I go down a few weeks afterwards and am offered a bargain and suppose, being from north of the Tweed, I am a shrewd bargainer and I buy for $90 what the ordinary American is paying $100 for, when I get to the customs house the Canadian government charges me the whole difference between $90 and $100. The government penalizes me for having followed my national instincts. Then after having charged me the full difference between $90 and $100 it imposes the tariff of 10 per cent, so I pay $20 on that importation of $90 instead of $9 as I should have paid. Before this change in the regulation, if I had only succeeded in getting a bargain for $95, the dumping clause would not have applied and I would have paid only the 10 per cent on the $95. But now, even if I get a bargain of 2 per cent I am going to be charged that 2 per cent, with the duty oh top of it.

The next step I want to see taken is the removal of the right of the Minister of Customs to value arbitrarily imports of natural products. That is a direct infringement of the right of parliament to impose taxation. It is open to the most serious abuse. It is protectionism of the most virulent and unwholesome character.
The third step I wish to see taken is the elimination of the valuation of goods at arbitrary values, such as valuing goods which come from one country at the supposed price that they are selling at in another. It is not a wholesome way of valuing goods. As a matter of fact, this depreciation of currency business has been altogether exaggerated. When you depreciate currency you raise prices. The German mark has practically disappeared-the old, paper mark; they have a new currency which they call the rentemark. I am told on reliable authority that prices in Germany to-day are what they were in 1914, plus about from 50 to 70 per cent. After all in the long run this endeavouring to enrich oneself by the issue of paper money defeats its own ends. It may have some temporary effect, but it is an effect which will be very temporary indeed.

perfectly clear. We will never import anything into this country that we can make more cheaply in Canada. We will never import into Canada anything which is not

The Budget-Mr. Hughes
better value for our money than something we can buy inside. The labour and capital of this country can best be employed in creating the value which is to be exchanged Mr. Speaker, if we could only eliminate the idea of money from peoples' heads and hearts and minds, we would get a much truer idea of what national trade is. It is barter between individuals, and no man gets poorer by getting bargains, no man gets poorer by exchanging what he has for something of more value. And as the nation is composed of individual units, no nation can get poorer by exchanging what it has for something of greater value.
Our manufacturers have had the tariff so long that some of them really believe that their very life blood depends on it. I think they are wrong. Prior to the emancipation of the slaves in the United States the greatest part of the public opinion of the southern states held as a unit that without negro slavery no economic life was possible in that part of the United States. They said that without the negroes to cultivate the cotton there was no future for the southern states as a whole. Ministers from their pulpits justified negro slavery; college professors from their chairs stated that without negro slavery the economic life of the south could not go on. But negro slavery was fundamentally unjust, even as it is fundamentally unjust to maintain protection in a country where there the vast body of the people cannot be protected. The feeling that negro slavery was unjust and unrighteous steadily grew. It grew first in the north; the abolitionists were reviled and prosecuted, but their influence increased until the nation trusted and the nation tried. They did away with slavery, and only after a bloody war; but did the southern United States go down? They went down for a while under the turmoil of the reconstruction period, for which carpet-baggers from the north were as much responsible as the southerners, perhaps more so. But the tremendous development of the southern states would have been impossible under slavery. In the same way I say that nothing that is just can be inexpedient, and by following the dictates of prudence, animated by the spirit of justice, desirous of getting rid of special privilege, we may be confident that the future of Canada, not only nationally but economically, is assured.

The Conservatives are confident that they have the government at a disadvantage, no matter what its policy may be. No matter what the government might do, whether its policies are in the interest of the country or not, no matter how wise or beneficial its legislation might be, it was going to receive the condemnation of the official opposition. But there is worse than that. A paper published in my own province, strongly supporting the Conservative party, a paper which in an issue some time ago stated that the present leader of the Conservative party was the ablest statesman now living in the world, in an editorial referring to the threatened strike of the post office employees a few weeks ago said:
As for the opposition, well, they rather enjoy seeing the government embarrassed, let the trouble come from whatever quarter it may.

speechtext:
I have read the speech
of the ex-Minister of Finance very carefully, and on page 1223 of Hansard he made this statement:
We would further expect something to be done to help the Canadian farmer, who to-day is shut out from his natural market to the south.
From his natural market to the south 1 Whenever Liberals have said that our natural market was to the south, they were accused of being disloyal. When did the Conservative party come to the conclusion that our natural market was to the south? Was this statement made by my hon. friend in a moment of candour, or because of a sudden ray of light, or was it simply an accident? In the year 1911, when the reciprocity agreement was negotiated with the United States, when this natural market was thrown open to the producers of Canada, to the natural industries of this country, my hon. friend and his associates adopted every device and made every statement they could think of to deceive and mislead the Canadian people in regard to that matter. WThen those negotiations were being conducted the legislature in the province from which I come was in session. The leader of the Conservative party introduced a resolution stating that the people of Prince Edward Island were in favour of a fair measure of reciprocity with the United States. Another Conservative seconded that resolution and it was passed unanimously. Two or three months later when that reciprocity agreement came before the people of Canada the Conservative party in the federal parliament decided to oppose it. These same gentlemen went out upon the hustings and declared that the agreement that had been negotiated would be ruinous to that province and to the whole of Canada. I asked these gentlemen, in view of the fact that they had put themselves on record as being in favour of reciprocity, could they come to the conclusion that the agreement as reached was not fair? Was there any feature of it not fair? I got no answer. I asked, wTas there any item on the reciprocal list that should not be there, and I got no answer. I asked them to tell me if there was any item on the list that should be removed, and I could not get an answer. The attitude of the Conservative party in Prince Edward Island was a fair sample of the attitude of the Conservative party throughout Canada.
As I have already stated, I read carefully the speech made by the ex-Minister of. Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and I find he

The Budget-Mr. Hughes
stated that the reductions in the tariff provided in the budget were made at the behest of the farmers or the Progressive party-in this House; and in the same breath he stated that the reductions that had been made, or the changes that had been proposed, would be of no benefit to the farmers of the country. Although they were made at the request of the farmers' party and were satisfactory to the representatives of the rural constituencies, he declared that they were of no advantage to them. He actually stated that the reductions amounted to the small sum of only $750,000; yet at the same time he said that they would destroy the manufacturing and industrial interests of the country. In the next place he stated that the manufacturers of agricultural implements were the only people who would benefit by the changes. The hon. ex-Finance Minister laughs. He has reason to.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, indeed you have. Considerable effort is being made in the country and by the Conservative members in this House to mislead and deceive the people engaged in farming and in the production of agricultural products. The province of Prince Edward Island has made a great success of the poultry branch of the farming business. They have also made a success of other branches of farming, and I find the newspapers in the province from which I come are particularly stressing what they call an argument, namely the fact that the United States charge a customs duty of eight cents a dozen upon eggs going into that country, while we, in Canada charge but three cents, and they claim that this is a great injustice to the poultrymen and farmers of this Dominion. We have only to examine the production in this country and the exports and imports of eggs to satisfy ourselves that a higher duty on that commodity would be of no advantage whatever to the poultrymen or farmers of Canada. The estimated production of eggs in Canada is $48,000,000 to $50,000,000 a year. We import $2,000,000 worth and export very nearly $2,000,000 worth. It is a seasonal product. We import eggs largely at the season of the year when we are not producing them here. It is a product the people want to get if possible in a fresh state, and can anybody say that to place a duty on the small amount we are importing at a season when the farmers and poultrymen have no fresh eggs to sell, in the months of December, January and February, could be of any possible advantage to the poultrymen or farmers of this country.
The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) referred to the article of cheese a few days ago when speaking on the budget, and intimated that the farmers of the Dominion of Canada were at a great disadvantage and were suffering a great hardship because the duty on cheese coming into the country was not higher, while at the same time our exports of cheese are about 1,000 per cent greater than our imports. We only import a small quantity of cheese of a particular kind that we do not produce in this country. The farmers of Canada have entire control of the local market and export a very large quantity. The estimated value [DOT]of the cheese produced in Canada in 1922 ,was $28,000,000. In that year we imported $325,000 worth and we exported $25,440,000, and the same with regard to butter. An effort has been made to show the farmers, particularly in the Maritime provinces from which I come, that they are being injured because there is not a greater duty on butter.
I presume that the Americans have a higher customs duty on butter than we have, but we have the butter market well in hand, and the statement I have here covers only creamery butter and takes no account of the private dairy. We produced in 1922 $53,000,000 worth of butter, we imported only $1,000,000, we exported $5,000,000, and we took care of the home market completely.
I have listened to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) and other hon. gentlemen who tell us that a protective policy, with high customs duties, is of great advantage to the people of this part of the country, that is to the people of Ontario and to the western part of Quebec. A day or two ago I read in the Montreal Gazette an editorial commenting on a letter received from a farmer in the county of Middlesex stating that the home market was of very great advantage. I will take at their face value the statement of that newspaper, the statement of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the statements of other hon. gentlemen who represent constituencies in the neighbourhood of Toronto and other Ontario cities, or constituencies in the neighbourhood of Montreal, and who tell us that the markets they find in those cities are a very great advantage to them. But I want in fairness to tell those hon. gentlemen that the men who profit by those home markets, by this protection, are the men who should bear the burden, I do not care how it is adjusted. I have no fault to find with any municipality, or city or province that wishes to bonus manufacturing industries. I think the people who profit by that system should pay the piper. What I object to is that
The Budget-Mr. Hughes

the people whom I represent, the people who live in the Maritime provinces, and particularly the people who live in Prince Edward Island, who never will, never did and never can benefit by those markets, should be called upon to pay their share of the cost of the music and the refreshments. The same is true with regard to western Canada. There is in my opinion no other country in the world where a system of protection could do less injury than in the country to the south of us, a compact country with every variety of climate, every variety of production. The people of that country could, if necessary, five and trade within themselves. On the other hand, there is no country in America, either north or south, and I doubt if there is a country in the world where protection will do as much harm as in the Dominion of Canada, because of our geographical position and because of the fact that our productions are very much of the same character in every province.
The farmers and fishermen of the Maritime provinces-I do not care what the transportation rates may be-cannot enter the markets of this part of Canada. Their natural market lies to the south, in the United States, or in the West Indian Islands, or in the island of Cuba, and very cogent and sensible observations, when we were discussing the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, were made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) in regard to conditions that he found in the West Indian Islands. He found that Canada was not represented by any trade agent or trade commissioner; that no effort was made to get the products of the Maritime provinces introduced into that part of the world. There is nothing in my opinion that the Department of Trade and Commerce could do that would benefit the Maritime provinces more than to send a few properly experienced business men to the West Indian Islands and to the island of Cuba to introduce our products there, to speak to their business men as a business man could, to represent our conditions and to enable us to enter those markets. They want our goods and we want theirs. That is the way that the provinces by the sea could be benefited. The farmers in this part of Canada can take care of all their home market that is now or will be available here for decades to come.
About two and one-half years ago when the present government came into office, what was the condition of things in Canada? We were going into debt at the rate of about a hundred million dollars a year. The last year the Conservative party was in power, the increase in the public debt was $92,000,000, and if they had not taken advantage of the issue of bonds by
'Mr. Hughes.1
the Canadian National Railways, which they say now should be charged1 to the consolidated revenue fund, their deficit that year would have been at least $117,000,000. At that time, there were in Canada many people who were alarmed at the fact that we were taking over the Canadian National Railways, this tremendous burden. No daylight was seen; but in the short space of two years, it has been clearly demonstrated that within two or three years from now the Canadian National Railways will be no longer a liability, but an asset, able to take care of all its fixed operating expenses and fixed charges, and that it will probably be earning a surplus which can be used for reducing transportation costs or paying the interest upon the money or, at least, a part of the money lent by the government.
In two years the present government has succeeded in making a balanced budget. Even taking the word of their opponents, even taking the criticism offered this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the fact remains that the budget has, at all events, been balanced. If you take the system of book-keeping that has been followed in this country since confederation, there is a reduction in the debt of twenty to thirty million dollars. For the first time since reductions were made by the former Liberal government, there is an actual reduction in taxation. Nobody would have predicted some two years ago that any government coming into power at that time, shouldering all the burdens that this government had to shoulder, with high taxation, an enormous debt and deficits going on from year to year, would be able to change all that within the short space of two years. Only to-day I read an editorial in the Montreal Gazette which no Canadian could read *without a feeling of pride. speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion of the budget during the last few days. My hon. friends to the right seem to be much concerned over the few reductions that have been made in the tariff and they have been painting gloomy pictures of the deplorable state in which our infant industries are struggling at the present time. These pictures portray the factories as in a condition that is compelling them to close, with consequent ruin and distress; and the pity of it all is, that what seems to affect our good friends most vitally is the fact that the agricultural people are losing their home markets. It is suggested that when the farmers lose these markets the agricultural industry will no longer be able to exist. These gentlemen appear to appreciate the importance of this industry and pretend to be greatly interested in its welfare. Now, they claim that a saving of three-quarters of a million dollars in the tariff will not amount to anything from the standpoint of the agricultural interests, and yet at the same time, strange to say, they want us to believe that the loss of this sum will absolutely put the manufacturing industries out of business in the Dominion. Let me inform them that the farmers are thankful for small mercies. I do not suppose that this amount of money represents much to the industries of the East, but it surely' is a quite tidy sum in the eyes of the farmers to-day under existing conditions. The consternation that seized the minds of gentlemen of the Conservative party on the afternoon the budget was brought down appeared to be reflected to a rather remarkable extent in the infant industries in the remote parts ot some of the provinces. It was reported that one industry at least had collapsed during that afternoon, and later in the week it was found that there was slight hope for its recovery. The calamity howling this year seems to be coming entirely from the other
corner of the House; it is coming from those whom we have always regarded as Canadian statesmen, men who are directly interested in the welfare of Canada and not in any particular section or class of our people. I say, the blue ruin cry is coming entirely from that vicinity. The manufacturers themselves are raising the same cry, and the press of our country seems to be heralding these sad tidings I have heard of individuals spending a week in the city of Toronto on Sunday but it seems that some of our manufacturing friends have spent almost fifteen years withm the short space of time since this budget came down. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association held a meeting in Toronto recently; it, is astonishing how quickly the effect of the budget seems to have been brought about.
I quote from the Montreal Gazette the following statements:
Mr. Winslow, of the Canadian Ingersoll Rand Drill Company, Sherbrooke, said the budget, so far as his firm was concerned, read like a sheet of their catalogue with severe reductions on everything they made. For 30 years their firm had been one of the leading industries at Sherbrooke, and should employ in normal prosperous times about 1,000 hands. They were now employing about 350, with prospects of a speedy decrease.	.	.
"They had a powerful American connection in the Ingersoll Rand," and like other businesses we must get our products where we can get them cheapest, whether we manufacture in Sherbrooke or Philipsburg. With the reduction in duty on our output and no drawback on raw material it looks to me very much as though the rock drill industry in Canada is about to be dosed down, because this budget hits us very hard.
Sir Alexander Bertram said he had been in the manufacturing business for 50 years, largely selling machinery and tools to the agricultural machinery industry, but with many of their customers for the past 15 years they had not sold a tool, because of the decline of the
industry.	.
W. R. Granger, Montreal, said the alleged farmers oi the West had organized politically, and he thought it time the C.M.A. stopped soft pedalling on politics, and turned to the loud pedal. He thought they ought to start work at once on this, and also on an educational propaganda, while he considered the proposed resolution quite too weak. "What we want to do," he argued, "is to get into as good a position as the Progressives have, so that we can have some weight in Parliament behind our demands." (Applause.)
The whole gist of the report seems to be that the trouble is altogether attributable to tariff reductions, especially to those which this budget will put into effect. I am giving these quotations merely to show the House the ignorance of the people who are discussing fiscal affairs. Further down I notice that Mr. Wilkins, of Farnham, argued:
The political grain growers of the West were not farmers such as we have in the East, doing their grain mining by contract, and spending the winters in the south. This province consumes almost all its own agricultural products, and he believed 96 per cent of the Quebeckers were protectionists.
The Budget-Mr. Milne

Last season while the special committee on Agriculture was sitting one of the witnesses made bold to assert that the farmers of the West should feed steers in the winter instead of going South and enjoying the warmer climate. When he was questioned closely as to how many western farmers he knew who spent their winters in the South- and he was a man who had had quite a broad experience throughout the Dominion -he admitted that he had heard of but one farmer who went South to escape the Canadian winter. We have heard a great deal about the peaceful rural population of Quebec. For many years I envied their contentment and prosperity-or rather the glowing accounts of it which I read from time to time. But I found on making an examination-and it is now a well-known fact-that the exodus of young native born Canadians from the province of Quebec is proportionately as great as from our other provinces. Consequently, I have come to the conclusion that although the Manufacturers' Association may have good intentions, they are very, very ill informed as to actual existing conditions.
Lately we have heard a good deal about our implement manufacturers being in sore straits, and we are led to believe that the whole trouble is due to their not having sufficient protection. On the other hand we have been told that the United States were building up a tariff wall higher than ever in order to stimulate their industries and create national prosperity. In this connection it is interesting to learn of the actual conditions on the other side, and therefore I quote the following from the Literary Digest:
One organization that realizes to the full the extent of farm distress during the last two or three years is the National Association of Farm Equipment Manufacturers. The Manufacturers' Record, Baltimore, shows that the production in 1922 of farm implements was about one-third or one-half, and in some cases even less, of that in 1914.	'
Further on appears the following:
According to the association's circular twenty of the leading companies have lost $50,000,000 in two years.
To emphasize	that statement a	table is
given showing the actual production of a few of the principal agricultural implements in 1914 compared with the reduced production in 1922. I quote the following:

I refrain from reading the full list. It is very long, but there has been practically the 
same proportionate reduction of output in regard to all farm implements. This shows quite conclusively that the manufacturers of agricultural implements in the United States are not in a prosperous condition, notwithstanding that they have a supposedly model tariff to stimulate industry.
During the recess we have been bombarded with literature asking for tariff protection. I do not want to spend time in discussing it, but I must frankly confess that the men who are directing some of our industries fall very low in my estimation if the type of letters they have been sending out is any indication of their executive ability. In all the circulars which have reached me there is a strong plea for protection and yet not one of these men will tell us the actual condition of his business. The general tone of the letters indicates an intention to raise prices. There is no apparent desire at all to lower the prices of their products the whole argument being that they must raise prices in order to continue in business. One sentence from such a circular letter will make this very clear. By the way the particular paragraph I am about to quote does not deal with the tariff, but with the sales tax, which the writer wants dropped on certain products of his factory. But this is the sentence:
This sales tax will have the effect of curtailing consumption, thereby causing the manufacturer to again increase prices to meet his bills.
If we follow this through to its logical conclusion we find that eventually there will be no sales at all. By that time I feel convinced that the individuals who are responsible for this propaganda will have become exceedingly bold, and will be asking the government to subsidize them in order that they may pay their executives salaries from $25,000 to $30,000 presumably on the ground that they are consumers of agricultural products! I repeat, it is unfortunate that throughout all this special pleading for protection there is not one instance of these men attempting to show [DOT]the actual necessity of protection for their particular business.
Last session several industrial managers appeared before the' special committee on Agriculture. We had before us the manager of the Massey-Harris Company. Now, I hold no grudge against the Massey-Harris Company; I wish them every success. But if they need protection, why were they so slow, why did they not give the committee the facts as to how their capital stock was made up and what their profits and dividends had been over a period of years0 These things were

The Budget-Mr. Milne
kept almost entirely in the dark. The closest we got to it was the information elicited from one witness that between 1913 and 1920 the capital stock had been augmented by $4,000.000 and that of this amount only about $160,000 was new capital. If that kind of thing is going on it is no wonder they are not able to pay dividends.
We had before us another witness, the manager, I think it was, of the Canadian Ford Company. They were very frank in their statements. I shall not weary the House with a statement of the whole financial standing of the company, but I should like to give an example of how an investment in ten shares amounting to $1,000, made in 1907, had increased in 1923 to a value of $310,010. During that period this $1,000 invested, as I say, in 1907, had paid a cash dividend of $32,810 and had increased in stock to the amount of 560 shares, worth at that time $270,200, making the total I have mentioned, $310,010. That, it seems to me was a pretty good investment.
I noticed in Saturday Night a few weeks ago a report with regard to one of our industries, Canadian Steel. I will read a few extracts from this report just to give you an idea of the peculiar circumstances pertaining to that company. The report says:
The annual report for the year ending December 31, 1923, demonstrates that the Steel Company of Canada is once more on the upgrade in earnings. It won its way into a very enviable position during the war as evidenced by the fact that the profit and loss surplus, which stood at $3,014,642 at the end of 1915, had become $8,740,966 at the end of 1920 in spite of the fact that it paid in every subsequent year dividends on both preferred and common stocks, seven per cent on the preferred and four, six and seven per cent progressively on the common, the latter figure having been maintained since 1919. The huge surplus mentioned was shaved a little in 1921 and 1922 decreasing respectively to $8,298,517 and $7,942 372. But 1923 earning results showed a balance of $627,875.40, after paying all expenses and fixed charges and making the ample provisions considered necessary for various sinking funds and reserves, and this sent the profit and loss surplus once more skiting up to $8,570,247.75. This means an entire recovery of the ground lost in 1921 and 1922 and brings the surplus up within hail of the high point achieved in 1920. Another year like 1923, and it will be in a position unexampled for strength in its own line in Canada.
Add to this its various reserves, standing as follows:	furnace relining and rebuilding reserves, $792,-
972.68; reserves for accidents to employees, $84,811.82; contingent reserve, $546,667.23; betterment and replacement reserve, $1,885,953.82; fire insurance reserve, $200.000; bond and sinking fund reserve, $1,737,748.92; and depreciation account, $7,048,508.28, making a total of $12,296,662.75. At the end of 1915 these reserve funds only totalled $1,257,811.
Further on it speaks of paying off some other liabilities as they came due. From that I think you will see that the industry
is not suffering very much so far as profits are concerned.
A few years ago some of us heard of an industry that had been built up not for the glory of God but for the profits of the shareholders, and it was declared that that industry had in 1918 made a profit of 291 per cent. That is just an example of the condition of some of the industries that are asking for protection. Some of our industries may not be in a very good position. I am not going to say whether they are or whether they are not, because they have not given full information with respect to the actual conditions as they exist. In this connection I do not see why I should not offer a few suggestions to our manufacturing friends, because they are not backward in offering suggestions to the agriculturists, and I think I can say without boasting that I am probably just as well fitted to give a little advice to our manufacturing friends as some of them are to advise the agriculturists. We had before our committee last year an analysis of the cost of a binder. The costs of material, wages, and so on, were considered separately, and a comparison was made between the costs in 1913 and those in 1922. I will just read the figures; they are very interesting.

That shows a total of $359.99 for 1922 as against $163.99 for 1913. The thing that strikes me there is that the factory expenses and administration have increased beyond all proportions. We are usually told that it is labour that is keeping the price of our implements up, but we find here that the factory expenses and administration have enormously increased. I submit that there is just as much reason for the practice of economy on the part of the manufacturers, as well as the study of more economical production, as there is on the part of the agriculturists.
I have been looking over a report with respect to the pulp and paper industry prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and a startling thing to me is the number of officers and superintendents, and the amount of money that goes to them in salaries. The number of officers and superintendents amounts to one sixtieth of the total number of employees, and they draw one-eleventh of the total wages. It looks to me
The Budget-Mr. Milne

as if that was rather out of proportion. In addition to the officers and superintendents there are technical experts and clerk stenographers whom I put in along with the common labourer, and it looks as if there was room for same paring in officers and superintendents. I do not wish to leave a wrong impression. I am absolutely in favour of a man drawing a salary in proportion to his ability. I am not one of those who think that every one should be paid the same wage or salary, but I am of the opinion that many of our industries are loaded down with officers who are not much more than parasites.
In looking over another return from the same source, prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce, I find that in the hosiery and knitted goods industry the number of employees on salary has increased from the year 1920 to 1921 by 20 per cent, whereas the number of wage earners has increased by only 7 per cent. As I said before, I do not know the reason for that, and I am not able to go any further, but it seems to me that the management cannot be as efficient as it might be. Another place where a good deal of work needs to be done, and it should be done by our friends, is in the matter of distribution. The present system is extremely costly and inefficient. I believe there are millions spent on advertising that is an absolute waste, and in that connection I want to read just a short extract from the evidence of a witness who was before the committee last year, a manufacturer who lives very close to this city. Speaking of a report by Congressman Anderson he said-
My view is and it was before I read this, that the retailer has to a certain extent lost his function, and I am going to make another statement that I know will be challenged outside of here, if it should receive any publicity, that is that one of the tremendous economic ills of this country and of the United States as wed, is national advertising. There are hundreds of millions of dollars spent in advertising for which there is no economic return. I contend I have studied the question, and that advertising is an advantage to the advertiser. He makes money out of it. It pays to advertise and it pays the medium of advertising. While I am on that, I would say it has enabled the newspapers to pay more for their editors and employees, and it may be a good thing for the newspaper.
I hat is what Mr. Sparks says about advertising, and I agree with him heartily. I maintain that our industries have a great big field to work in so far as a more economic distribution of their goods is concerned. I do not confine that to the manufacturing industry at all, for the same thing applies to our agricultural products, which are not in my opinion marketed in an efficient manner. We had our attention drawn last year to the fact that apples for which the producer received $4 a barrel were retailed at the equivalent of $27

a barrel, and many similar instances were given. We found that the farmer who was milking his cows twice daily got five cents a bottle for his milk, while the distributor in the city got six and a half cents. That seems to me altogether out of all proportion.
There is just one other thing I want to say by way of advice to the manufacturer. Let me suggest that you apply the same remedy to manufacturers as you recommend for agriculturists. If you are not making a profit out of the product of your factory, you are not making the right product; that is what they tell the farmers. If you cannot make any money turning out baby carriages, make automobiles. If you cannot make a profit manufacturing wagons, make sleighs. That may sound ridiculous, but it is just about as sensible and reasonable as the advice that is given to' the farmer from certain sources. I want to say that it is quite impossible for a farmer who has been making a specialty of growing grain to turn round immediately and produce d'airy products profitably. There is a real art in dairying if you are going to make a success of it, and the same is true of poultry. A man who is a good dairyman may not be able to make any money out of poultry. It is quite impossible for a farmer to immediately swing around from one type of farming to another successfully. It is almost as impracticable as to expect a manufacturer to turn from making baby carriages and make a success of manufacturing automobiles.
