I said, I should judge from
his question. I would like to give a quotation from the Agriculturist Gazette which is published in Ottawa by the Agricultural department. There seems to be a general impression that the farmers of the West are merely wheat growers or wheat miners as they are called. The impression is not well founded, and I think this quotation will perhaps serve to prove that as well as anything I know of.
In the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta the dairy industry has developed since 1910 in a remarkable manner. The output of creamery butter having increased from 4,161,947 pounds, valued at $459,254 in 1910, to 28,619,641 pounds, valued at $10,348,762 in 1921 A further increase in 1922 over 1921

The Budget-Mr. Milne
is recorded as follows: In Manitoba 23.5 per cent, Saskatchewan 25 per cent and Alberta 20 per cent.
I should think that would indicate that the agricultural people, even in the western provinces, were doing pretty well. What are the conditions that are confronting agriculture today? It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is no use in trying to delude ourselves in regard to actual conditions. We have heard much about the big crops that were produced in western Canada this year. We are told of the tremendous volume pouring into the ports and being exported from the country. But let us analyse this matter as far as the farmers are concerned. The total field crop production for 1923 was $892,572,300, in 1922 it was $962,616,200 and in 1921 it was $931,862,670. Hon. members will see that it is decreasing right along. Let us analyse it a little bit further. Take the commodity of wheat. We find that the production of wheat increased last year by a considerable amount. The production of wheat last year was estimated at a little over 474,000.000 bushels as against 399,000,000 bushels for the previous year. I have the figures for oats, barley and flax but I will not weary the House with them except to say that all down the line we have increased production in 1923 over 1922, but the value of our total production showed that it had decreased. It is decreasing right along. So far as the farmer is concerned, he is surely doing his part in producing the goods. These figures refer to field crops.
Now coming to diversified farming, I will deal first with the commodity of bacon. I took these figures from the Trade and Commerce reports ending March, 1923, so that when I say 1923 it is really not for the calendar year 1923. The amount of bacon exported in
1922	amounted to 992,080 hundredweight, and in 1923 it was 1,015,901 hundredweight. Hon. gentlemen will notice that there was an increase in the amount, but when we come to the value in 1922 it was $23,012,480 and in
1923	it was $22,536,397. Then the live cattle exported in 1922 amounted to 161,483 head and in 1923 to 229,080 head. That showed an increase in the export of live cattle of 42 per cent. The value of our exports in 1922 was $7,852,111, and in 1923, $8,738,243, or an increase in the value of only 11 per cent. In the commodity of butter we show an increase of 260 per cent in volume and 255 per cent in the returns. In the matter of cheese we have a decrease of 85 per cent in volume and 82 per cent in returns. Now if we sum up the whole agricultural industry as it is summed up in the agricultural statistical bulletin we find that we have a total value for agriculturelands, buildings and so on-of $6,744,000,000 and we find that the gross revenue was $1,420,000,000. These figures are so large that it is almost impossible to grasp their meaning. According to the last census returns we had 798,360 farmers in Canada. We divide our gross revenue and find out what each farmer gets, and it amounts to about $1,700 per farm. It was estimated that the taxes, Dominion, federal, provincial and municipal amounted to about $100 per individual, with an average family of five, so that it would make $500 of a tax bill to start with. Now if we take the depreciation on the implements and buildings, we find that there is a depreciation of 10 per cent on implements and buildings, which I think is very fair. We have $142,737,000 of a depreciation there. If we allow 5 per cent on the total capital investment, that amounts to another $338,723,000. If we divide this for each farm we find an added cost again of about $600. So that if we take our interest and depreciation of $600 and taxes $500 we find we have about $600 per farm left. Out of that the farmer has to pay his hired help and buy his machinery, twine, and so on. That is the actual condition, I believe, so far as agriculture is concerned.
While our products increased in quantity, yet there was a decrease all along the line in value. Everybody is anxious to help the agricultural industry, and everybody i3 watching it. The manufacturers, the bankers, the railroads, the governments and every financial interest in the Dominion during the summer have their fingers on the pulse of agriculture and a continuous study is being made of conditions. They realize the fact that a big crop or good returns means prosperity to them as well. I wonder if my hon. friends who are asking for protection sincerely believe that we in Canada must wait until our industries will build up so as to provide a home market for our agricultural products. I used to wonder why the buffalo were brought to the park at Wain-wright and left at the edge of the prairie, and I have just come to the conclusion that the idea was to turn them loose and let them roam up there when the western provinces are again depleted of the population that is there at the present time. That will be necessary, and a long period will intervene before we need to use those lands again if we have to wait for home markets for our agricultural products.
As regards the home market and the prices of our agricultural products, that does not amount to a hill of beans. We find that the butter market at Montreal, which, I under-
The Budget-Mr. Milne

stand, is regulated by the export market, is the determining factor of the price of our dairy products. We find that the price of our wheat and other grain is determined by the price of grain at Liverpool. I cannot see why we agriculturists should be fooled by waiting for and expecting great prosperity when we get a huge industrial Canada that will consume more of our products. What has been done that will ' benefit agriculture, that primary industry which produces nearly one-half of our total exports? What has been done that will make it more prosperous? Last year I think we had a modest prayer from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in which he remarked that if we had a good crop, the West would be prosperous again. The West had one good crop last year; nobody can dispute the fact that we had a big crop, and yet conditions are apparently not very much better. We also had a kick in the ribs from the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie), who said that if farmers improved production by improving herds, they could pay the duty on their agricultural implements. That was the sympathy he gave. A little further on in his speech he was speaking of conditions and the time when pea fed hogs were sold for 2J cents a pound. He said:
I venture to think that these conditions produced better citizenship than are produced to-day by all the spoon feeding done by federal, provincial and municipal governments.
I have been trying to appreciate what he meant and what he was getting at, but for the life of me I cannot understand when the farmers have been spoon fed. Spoon feeding is the very thing we are trying to get away from. Our industries have been spoon fed for the last forty years and they are taking' it well yet. Why remarks like that should be directed at agriculturists is beyond my comprehension. There seems to be an impression in eastern Canada that when a delegation from one of the eastern provinces appears at Ottawa asking for something, they are demanding simply their rights, whereas, when a western deputation appears, it is trying to grab off something at the expense of the remainder of the country. This, it seems to me, is a peculiar attitude to take. We are told by a good many that we are blind; that protection is not the cause of all our troubles. We do not for a moment think that protection is the cause of all our troubles. We are different from our protectionist friends in that respect. They think, if they lose their protection, they are absolutely lost; that there is nothing that hurts them but the lowering of duties.
The solution to our problems, it seems to me, lies in two sources. I am not one of those who believe that the government can

bring about prosperous times over night or in a year or in a couple of years. I am not one of those who believe that the agriculturists should lie down on their oars and not try to help themselves. Both have an important part to fill, and I am not going to deal here with the part that the agriculturists themselves have to play. We have to have cheaper production, and the farmer can do something towards helping that situation himself by improving his methods and so on as best lie possibly can- The government can help us in that respect by lowering the tariff and giving us cheaper implements of production and cheaper equipment to carry on our industry with.
We also need cheaper transportation. At the present time, it costs about 33 per cent of the value of a steer to take him from Saskatoon to the Liverpool market. Thirty-three per cent of the value of a steer is used up in transportation. We must do everything we possibly can to bring about lower freight rates. We must develop our ocean ports at the most strategical points. I think in this regard I might mention the Hudson Bay railway which the West is asking for, and I notice, from a report in the paper the other day, that the ex-Premier of Manitoba stated that he believed 95 per cent of the western people were behind him in the belief that the Hudson Bay route was feasible and that it should be given a trial. With the vast amount of money that has been spent there already and the small amount that it will take to give it a trial, it seems to me that it should be tried out. When I suggest development along those lines, I do not mean to develop politically; I do not mean to build elevators where there is no grain to ship; I do not mean to build dry docks where there are no boats to dock. I think conditions are more serious at this time than they ever were in the history of our Dominion and they should be given earnest consideration. In particular, freight rates have been unreasonably high, and yet Canadian shippers are protected by coastal regulations. We find that our products are being discriminated against in ocean transportation. We appear to find ourselves somewhat helpless in this matter, but I do not see why we should not keep up a vigorous howl until we get redress along that line too. It is unreasonable to expect that the Canadian farmer can pay more for taking his goods to the British market than his friend the American farmer. Why should two sacks of flour in the same hold bear a different rate while they are crossing the Atlantic ocean? That seems to me to be extremely ridiculous.

The Budget-Mr. Milne
I intended to deal somewhat with rural credits. It is too late, I am afraid, to save a number of our farmers. Many of our farmers to-day are bankrupt, and the only thing left is to assist them through the bankruptcy court and then to turn around and give them the assistance which new immigrants into our country are receiving. Then they will have a new start. They will know the conditions and they will make much better progress than will new immigrants that come in.
We have another class of farmers who are apparently still solvent, but whose credit is exhausted. I do not know what we can do with those, but I certainly think that the government made a big mistake when they practised economy on the Agricultural Instruction Act. These are the people who could be helped in this way by putting men in the field and enabling them to change their system wherever it was possible to do so. If this were done the morale of these people could be stimulated to such an extent that in a great many instances they would do considerably better. Then we have others who still have a little credit left. I am pretty well convinced that if conditions continue as they are at present our farmers' credit will soon have been exhausted; certainly they cannot continue paying 8 to 10 per cent interest on their money. If the government can borrow money at 5 per cent, I see no reason why the farmer should have to pay between 8 and 10 per cent. I know what the argument is:	It is
contended that there is a risk in lending money to the farmer and consequently the rate must be increased. But that strikes me as a most absurd argument, because the higher the rate the greater the risk must be. Where will you stop? At present the farmers of western Canada are making an heroic effort to launch one of the greatest marketing schemes ever undertaken and I think the government would be well advised to assist them to the extent of giving back to those provinces the money that rightfully belongs to them in order that they may be able to carry on this work that they have begun. I refer to the money left by the Wheat Board of 1919. They are trying to help themselves, but they are handicapped through lack of finances, notwithstanding that their own money is lying in the treasury here and is refused them.
The establishment of agriculture on a sound basis is to my mind a truly national problem. We were never before in such a serious condition as we are in at the present
time, and the time has come when every one should cast aside political prejudices so that all might sit around the table in cooperation. The manufacturers, the farmers, the lumbermen and the representatives of all other industries in the country should get together in an effort to solve this great problem. This country, I think, is undertaking a tremendous experiment in connection with agriculture. We heard a great deal yesterday from the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) in regard to the development that has taken place in highly protected countries. But the hon. gentleman did not tell us anything about the peasantry in those countries. The Dominion of Canada and the United States are engaged in one of the biggest experiments known to history, and we- are trying to carry on agriculture without any such peasantry. Agriculture is one of the noblest callings that a man can follow, and there is no reason why we should be ashamed of it. There is no reason why we should have to adopt any low standard of living. The farmers of this country and of the country to the south of us are determined to improve the conditions of agriculture and they will not tolerate any standard of living below that to which they are justly entitled. They are going to make agriculture an industry that they may be proud of. The experiment, I say, is a tremendous one, and I hope sincerely that our protectionist friendis will not follow the example of other countries and throw upon our agricultural people such burdens as will impoverish them and make a peasant race of this fair Canada of ours.
